There was none of the drama of the reverse fixture at the Gtech back in December, when Brentford had clawed back to 3-1 before Sauer's stoppage-time penalty settled it. This time the Racecourse got the version of Wrexham that has become the away sides' worst fixture list entry: patient in the first half, ruthless in the second, and never once looking like a team that needed to find a second gear. Yacel Amrizi broke the deadlock four minutes into the second half, latching onto a loose ball at the edge of the box and finishing low into the corner with the kind of composure that has made him close to automatic in this side's biggest matches.

The only real controversy of the afternoon arrived nineteen minutes in, when Leo Sauer was booked for a challenge on Brentford's right-back that the away bench felt merited more than a yellow. Sauer shrugged off the card and the complaints that followed it, and by the 79th minute he had turned the game's single moment of theatre into its decisive one — rising above a Brentford centre-back who had six inches on him to head home an Amrizi cross with the kind of leap that had Owen Meredith checking the replay twice from the press box. "I don't know where that came from," Sauer admitted afterward, laughing. "I'm not supposed to win those. Ask anyone in that dressing room — I get told to stay out of the air."

Racecourse Ground, Wrexham · Matchday 23
ResultWrexham 2–0 Brentford
ScorersY. Amrizi 49' · L. Sauer 79'
Y. AmriziMan of the Match · 7.8 rating
Premier LeagueP23 W16 D3 L4, 51 pts

It continues a pattern that has quietly defined this Premier League campaign: the club's two most expensive attacking signings, Amrizi and Sauer, delivering exactly the kind of moments the ownership group's spending was supposed to buy. Meredith has spent much of the season weighing that outlay against the academy graduates — Ngumoha, Mokio, Belghazi — who make up the spine of the same team, and Saturday's afternoon offered a reminder that the debate isn't really either-or. "You can build a squad on kids and still need someone who can finish from twelve yards under no pressure at all," Meredith wrote in his notes. "Wrexham have both right now, which is precisely why teams like Brentford are finding this fixture list so unforgiving."

Jenkins, asked about Sauer's card in the post-match press conference, was characteristically unbothered. "Leo plays right on the edge of what a referee will allow, and most weeks that edge is where he's most dangerous," he said. "I'm not going to coach that out of him for the sake of one afternoon. Not when he goes and does what he did for the second goal." Pressed on whether the header changed how he sees Sauer's role in the side, Jenkins allowed himself a rare grin: "I've told him to stay on the ground and let the big men handle crosses for two years now. Today he made me look silly. I'll live with that."

I've told him to stay on the ground and let the big men handle crosses for two years now. Today he made me look silly. I'll live with that.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

Three points that never felt in serious doubt push Wrexham to 51 from twenty-three, and the manner of it — comfortable from the first whistle rather than nervy until the last — will matter more to Jenkins than the scoreline itself. Sheffield United arrive at the Racecourse next, a side who will offer a very different kind of test of whether Saturday's ease was the platform for another sustained run or simply a good afternoon against tired opposition.

headline: Bobadilla Brace Sends Wrexham Past a Booed-Off West Ham, 4-0
dek: Four goals, four different threats, and a pressroom question that won't go away: is Jenkins's system a masterpiece, or is everyone just having a bad day against it?
body_html:
The London Stadium has never been a warm room for visitors, but the noise that greeted Wrexham on a wet Friday night carried a different edge to it — not nerves, not anticipation, just irritation. West Ham's home crowd had watched their side slip to eighth with three defeats in five, and four minutes were all it took for that irritation to curdle into something closer to open booing. Damián Bobadilla, arriving late into the box off a Jorthy Mokio cutback, side-footed Wrexham into a lead so early it barely registered as a shock by the time the away end had finished celebrating.

It never really became a contest after that. Leo Sauer doubled the lead just past the half-hour mark with a finish Owen Meredith described from the press box as "the kind of goal that makes a defence stop trusting its own shape," then turned provider himself early in the second half, threading the ball through for Rio Ngumoha to make it three. Bobadilla completed his brace four minutes later, and by full time the boos from three sides of the ground had gone quiet, replaced by the low murmur of a home crowd trying to work out how a promoted side has made this look so routine. "We didn't do anything different tonight," Bobadilla said afterward, picking up his second Man of the Match award of the season. "We press, we win it back high, we're clinical when it matters. That's every week now, not just tonight."

London Stadium, London · Matchday 22
ResultWest Ham 0–4 Wrexham
ScorersD. Bobadilla 4' · L. Sauer 38' · R. Ngumoha 56' · D. Bobadilla 60'
D. BobadillaMan of the Match · 8.1 rating
Premier LeagueP22 W15 D3 L4, 48 pts

It is becoming a familiar shape to these Wrexham away days, and Meredith has started asking the question out loud that the pressroom has been circling for weeks: is Keeyvon Jenkins's high press and quick-strike system actually a tactical masterpiece, or are teams simply having off nights against it in sequence? "You can call one bad performance an anomaly," Meredith wrote in his notes after the final whistle. "You can't call ten of them that. At some point the common denominator stops being the opponent and starts being Wrexham." A West Ham staffer, asked in the mixed zone whether tonight was uncharacteristic, was blunter still: "We prepared for their press all week. Didn't matter. They're quicker to every second ball than we were, every single time."

Jenkins, for his part, kept the tone level in the post-match press conference, deflecting credit toward a squad he has spent the season rotating without ever seeming to weaken it. "I'll let other people argue about what to call it," he said when Meredith put the masterpiece question to him directly. "What I know is that we've built a group where whoever plays, the identity doesn't change. That's not magic. That's a lot of Tuesdays on the training ground." It is, as Meredith noted wryly, exactly the kind of answer designed to end a line of questioning rather than feed it — but with Wrexham now unbeaten in three and finding goals from four different scorers in as many matches, the debate over how much of this is system and how much is talent shows no sign of going away.

We didn't do anything different tonight. We press, we win it back high, we're clinical when it matters. That's every week now, not just tonight.

— Damián Bobadilla, post-match

Wrexham's away form has quietly become one of the more remarkable threads of this maiden Premier League campaign — a promoted club that was supposed to find its legs tested hardest on the road instead treating trips like the London Stadium as routine business. Whether that holds up against sterner opposition later in the run-in remains the open question hanging over an otherwise comfortable night in east London.

headline: Chido Obi Tears Through Chelsea as Wrexham's Kids Reach Another Final
dek: A brace and an assist from the eighteen-year-old, plus full debuts in all but name for three of the club's newest academy graduates, and Wrexham are one match from a first major cup final in this ownership era.
body_html:
Stamford Bridge has not been kind to Wrexham's academy sides in the past, but on a cold Wednesday night Chido Obi decided the venue's history didn't apply to him. Two goals either side of half-time and a third laid on for Toni Fruk turned what looked, on paper, like a difficult away leg against a Premier League rival into a rout — Wrexham's fourth away-from-home statement performance of a season that keeps producing them. "He's frightening now," Jenkins said of his eighteen-year-old striker afterward. "Frightening for defenders, and I think frightening for us too, in a good way — because I'm not sure we've worked out how good he can be yet."

The scoreline will draw the headlines, but the team sheet told its own story. Nico Kopp started in goal, Jermaine Lord and Vittorio Martini both featured from the bench — the trio promoted from the Youth Academy that same week — and none of the three looked remotely overawed by the occasion. "You don't throw kids into a place like this unless you trust them," Jenkins said. "I trust them. The academy staff trust them. Now they just have to trust themselves, and tonight was a good night to start." Vladyslav Veleten added gloss late on with a fourth, capping a night where Chelsea's response — a deflected Dušan Vlahović strike just after the break — barely registered as a threat to the result.

Stamford Bridge, London · Semi Final Match 1
ResultChelsea 1–4 Wrexham
ScorersC. Obi 2 · T. Fruk 1 · V. Veleten 1
C. ObiMan of the Match · 8.8 rating, 2G 1A
DebutsN. Kopp (GK) · J. Lord · V. Martini

For a club whose recruitment strategy has leaned so heavily on buying raw potential from academies across Europe and South America, there was something pointed about winning a Wrexham-grown night like this. "People keep asking whether the American owners are just going to buy their way to the top," Obi said, half-smiling, when the question inevitably came up in the mixed zone. "Ask them again after tonight." It's the kind of line that will follow him around for a while — and one this column suspects he knew exactly what he was saying when he said it.

"You don't throw kids into a place like this unless you trust them. Tonight was a good night for them to start trusting themselves."

— Keeyvon Jenkins

A first leg lead this size should be close to unassailable, but Jenkins was careful afterward not to call it finished. "Four one is four one. It's not the final," he said. "We go again at home and we try to do it properly, not just defend a scoreline." With a first Carabao Cup final within reach for a club that measured its ambitions in League Two survival not so long ago, the second leg at the Racecourse now carries a weight few inside the club could have imagined when this ownership era began.

headline: Chido Obi's First Senior Hat-Trick — Actually a Four — Sinks Nottingham Forest
dek: A controlled afternoon at the Racecourse turned into a rout once Obi found his range, and a full debut for academy graduate Emiliano Bianchi added a second story to a comfortable FA Cup evening.
body_html:
Nottingham Forest arrived at the Racecourse as a top-flight side with nothing obviously to fear from an FA Cup tie away at Wrexham, and for periods of the first half that looked like a fair assessment. It stopped looking that way in the twelfth minute, when Chido Obi opened the scoring, and it had stopped being a contest at all by the time he'd added a third early in the second half. "Controlled from start to finish" was how Jenkins described it afterward, and for once the cliché undersold the performance rather than flattering it. "Chido gets one, and you can see the belief change in the whole team," Jenkins said. "When he's in that mood, we just try to get him the ball and stay out of his way."

Obi's fourth, in stoppage time, turned a very good night into a statement one — his first senior hat-trick, extended to four inside a single half of controlled, patient football. "I stopped counting after the second one," Obi admitted, laughing. "You don't say that out loud during the game, you just want the next one." Forest's consolation, a stray finish from Folarin Kalimuendo, barely dented the afternoon; by that point the Racecourse crowd had long since turned its attention to the bench.

The Racecourse, Wrexham
ResultWrexham 4–1 Nottingham Forest
ScorersC. Obi 4
C. ObiMan of the Match · 9.3 rating, 4 goals
DebutEmiliano Bianchi

Buried a little in the box score was a full debut for Emiliano Bianchi, the academy midfielder promoted alongside Marco Soria back in December, who came through an assured 66 minutes without looking remotely troubled by the step up. "He does the boring things well, which at his age is the most encouraging sign there is," Jenkins said of the Italian. "Wins the ball back, plays it simple, doesn't panic. That's a foundation you can build a career on." For a club whose academy pipeline has become as central to its identity as any marquee signing, another debut worth remembering — even on a night one teenager's finishing made sure nobody would remember much else.

"Chido gets one, and you can see the belief change in the whole team. When he's in that mood, we just try to get him the ball and stay out of his way."

— Keeyvon Jenkins

With Forest dispatched, Wrexham move on in the FA Cup carrying the same question the club has carried through every round of every competition this season: how far can a squad this young, playing with this little fear, actually go? Nobody at the club is answering that question out loud yet. Nobody needs to — the performances keep doing it for them.

headline: Wrexham Finally Play Like Themselves Again, and It's Enough to Beat Chelsea
dek: A week after the Brighton defeat threatened to sour the New Year, Jenkins's side found a different gear entirely — more the ball, fewer chances conceded, and a first win of 2027 built on patience rather than transition.
body_html:
Four days after Brighton ended a seven-week unbeaten run at the Amex, Keeyvon Jenkins had a decision to make: chase the same transition-heavy football that had carried Wrexham through the autumn, or try something else against a Chelsea side built to punish exactly that kind of game. He chose something else. For the first time in a long stretch of matches, Wrexham held the ball — 52% of it to Chelsea's 48% — and made their visitors do the chasing. "We talked about it all week," Jenkins said afterward. "We can't just be a team that waits and breaks. Against the good sides, sooner or later that stops working. Today we tried to be the team that dictates."

It showed in the numbers as much as the eye test. Wrexham had five shots to Chelsea's two, and 2.0 expected goals to Chelsea's 0.3 — a gulf that, on another afternoon, might have produced three or four goals rather than one. Instead it took until the second half for the pattern to pay off, Yacel Amrizi turning in a Rio Ngumoha cross for his thirteenth league goal of the season, a strike that owed as much to patient build-up as to Amrizi's usual instinct for being in the right place. "Rio put it on a plate," Amrizi said. "All I had to do was not miss it — which, some weeks, is easier said than done." Jenkins was more pointed about what the performance still lacked: "Two expected goals and we win by one. We have to be better in the box. That's not a coaching problem, that's a composure problem, and it's on the players to fix it as much as it's on me."

The Racecourse, Wrexham · Matchday 21
ResultWrexham 1–0 Chelsea
ScorersY. Amrizi 1 goal · R. Ngumoha 1 assist
L. CacaceMan of the Match · 7.6 rating
PossessionWrexham 52% · Chelsea 48%

Liberato Cacace, still adjusting to life at right-back a season and a half after his conversion from the left, was named man of the match for a display built on patience rather than the raw pace that used to define his game — timing his overlaps to the tempo of a possession-heavy afternoon rather than rushing every one. "Last season I would have bombed forward on the first chance and left a gap behind me," Cacace admitted. "Now I'm learning when not to go. That's the harder skill, honestly." It was the kind of unglamorous, structural performance that a slower, more controlled Wrexham needs more of if this style is going to stick beyond one afternoon.

There was a quieter subplot to the week, too. Kieffer Moore, last season's Player of the Year and the target man Wrexham built so much of their Championship promotion around, completed a £1.5m move to West Brom four days before kickoff — a player whose decline had become as much a fixture of matchday squads as his aerial threat once was. Nobody in the away end would have known the difference watching Wrexham's more patient approach against Chelsea, built now around Amrizi, Fruk, and Ngumoha rather than a target man at all. "Kieffer gave us Season 1," Jenkins said when asked about the sale. "This team owes him more than it can repay. But squads move on, and ours has outgrown the way we used to play around him." Whether that's true or simply the version of the story a manager tells after a sale is exactly the kind of question Meredith intends to keep asking as the second half of the season unfolds.

Two expected goals and we win by one. We have to be better in the box. That's not a coaching problem, that's a composure problem.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

The win moves Wrexham back into the top three and answers, for one match at least, the question Brighton had raised about whether this team could adapt when transition football stops working. West Ham away is next, a side who will offer Wrexham no such luxury of dictating tempo — the sternest test yet of whether Saturday's patience was a genuine evolution or a one-off against a Chelsea side having an off day.

headline: Al Dawsari Ends Wrexham's Unbeaten Run as the New Year Begins With a Thud at the Amex
dek: Three wins and a Carabao Cup shock of Manchester City had carried Wrexham into January full of momentum. A single second-half strike on the south coast was enough to stop it dead.
date_line: January 2, 2027 · The Amex, Falmer
body_html:
There is a particular flatness to a New Year's away trip on the south coast, squad legs still heavy from three matches in eleven days over Christmas, and Wrexham never quite shook it off at the Amex. Brighton, who had lost 1–0 to these same opponents back in September, set up cagier this time — deeper block, quicker to put bodies behind the ball whenever Amrizi got a yard of space — and for an hour it worked well enough to produce very little at either end. "We knew they'd set up different to the reverse fixture," Jenkins said afterward. "We didn't have an answer for it quickly enough, and against a team with nothing to lose that's usually when you get hurt."

They got hurt two minutes into the second half. Al Dawsari picked up a loose ball on the edge of the box after a half-cleared corner and curled it past Okonkwo before the visiting back line had reset — the kind of goal that punishes a slow restart rather than any sustained pressure. Wrexham pushed for an equalizer that never really threatened to arrive; Toni Fruk's half-chance from the edge of the box on the hour was the closest thing to a clear sight of goal all afternoon. "We didn't create enough to say we deserved something out of it," Fruk admitted in the mixed zone. "Some days the performance isn't there and you have to be honest about that instead of talking about bad luck."

The Amex, Falmer · Matchday 20
ResultBrighton 1–0 Wrexham
ScorerAl Dawsari 47' (opp.)
Premier League TableP20 W13 D3 L4, 42 pts · 3rd

It is the first defeat since Manchester City won 2–1 at the Racecourse on December 12th — a run that in between included a genuine statement result, beating a full-strength City side 2–0 in the Carabao Cup quarter-final with a youth-heavy XI just three days after that league loss. One of the few positives from an otherwise flat afternoon at the Amex was another look at Thiago Pitarch, signed from Real Madrid on transfer deadline eve, who came off the bench for his Wrexham debut and looked composed enough in a difficult half-hour to justify the fee nobody at the club will disclose. "He's not going to fix today on his own, but you could see the game slow down a little when he had it," Jenkins said of the midfielder. "That's the kind of calm we need more of when things aren't flowing."

We didn't create enough to say we deserved something out of it. Some days the performance isn't there and you have to be honest about that instead of talking about bad luck.

— Toni Fruk, post-match

The defeat drops Wrexham to third on goal difference, still very much inside the Champions League places with eighteen games to play, and a nine-day break before Chelsea visit the Racecourse gives Jenkins time to get the squad's legs back before the run resumes in earnest.

headline: Three Weeks I'd Take Again, and a Flight Home I Wouldn't
dek: From the low of losing to City to the Carabao Cup upset of the same club three days later, three straight league wins, and now a flat one to close it out — the whole thing in one stretch.
body_html:
Three weeks ago I wrote in here about the gap between us and City being smaller than people think but still real, and closing it being the whole job. Three days after I wrote that, we went to the Etihad with a team full of kids and beat their first XI 2–0 in the cup. I'm not going to pretend that result solved anything permanent — different competition, different stakes, different version of them on the touchline — but it told this group something true about itself that a league table can't: we're not scared of anybody in this country right now. We backed it up with three straight league wins over Brentford, West Ham, and Ipswich, and for about six days over Christmas we topped the Premier League table. I let myself feel that one properly this time.

And then today happened, and it's a useful correction to how good I was feeling. Brighton set up smart, we didn't have an answer quickly enough, and Dawsari punished the one mistake he needed. No City-level individual quality to point to this time — just a flat performance from a squad that's played a lot of football in a short window, on the road, in January, on the back of a result that maybe let a little air out of everyone without us noticing. Fruk said it best in the mixed zone: the performance wasn't there, and pretending otherwise doesn't help anybody. Pitarch's half-hour was the one thing I'll actually rewatch this week — calm on the ball in a game that badly needed someone calm on the ball.

We're not scared of anybody in this country right now. That's the real thing I take from the last three weeks — not the table position, which will move around plenty more before May.

— KJ

headline: Amrizi and Sauer See Off Ipswich as a Teenager Named Soria Gets His First Taste
dek: Wrexham survived a scare at Portman Road to stay in the Champions League places, while forty minutes down the touchline a home-grown eighteen-year-old made a first-team debut that cost the club nothing but four years of patience.
date_line: December 29, 2026 · Portman Road, Ipswich
body_html:
Portman Road on a wet Tuesday between Christmas and New Year is not where the Premier League's glamour lives, and for long stretches this did not look like a top-two fixture. Ipswich, bottom three and fighting for their lives, set up to make Wrexham as uncomfortable as a struggling side knows how — deep lines, bodies behind the ball, and a crowd that had waited all year for a Boxing Day-week banana skin. It nearly worked. "That's the hardest place we've played all season, and I include the away trips to City and Anfield in that," Jenkins admitted afterward. "When a team is fighting to stay up, they find something extra. We knew that going in."

Yacel Amrizi did what Yacel Amrizi does. Five minutes in, he turned a half-cleared corner into the opener, arriving at the back post ahead of two defenders who were still watching the ball in flight. Ipswich responded almost immediately — Davis Keillor-Dunn, once of this parish and still fondly remembered at the Racecourse for entirely different reasons, drilled a leveller past Arthur Okonkwo in the 12th minute that had the home end believing. The scrap that followed was scruffy, physical, and short on real chances until Leo Sauer, cutting inside from the left in the 65th minute, found the top corner from range to settle it. "We scraped it," Amrizi said flatly in the mixed zone, waving off a question about his goal involvement. "Away form in this league is decided by moments, not performances. We took ours, just about."

Portman Road, Ipswich · Matchday 19
ResultIpswich Town 1–2 Wrexham
ScorersY. Amrizi 5' · Keillor-Dunn 12' (opp.) · L. Sauer 65'
Y. AmriziMan of the Match · 1G 1A, 7.7 rating
Premier League TableP19 W13 D3 L3, 42 pts · 2nd

The result kept Wrexham in the Champions League places, but only just kept them there — Arsenal's own win elsewhere on the same day was enough to reclaim top spot on goal difference, a reminder that the club's brief run as Premier League leaders on Christmas Day lasted almost exactly ninety-six hours. Jenkins, when it was put to him, shrugged the framing off entirely. "I didn't take a phone call from anyone congratulating us for being top on the 25th, and I won't be taking one for being second on the 29th," he said. "Ask me in May."

The detail that will matter more in a year's time happened in the 66th minute, when Marco Soria — eighteen years old, signed into the academy as a raw, injury-interrupted prospect out of Córdoba back in March — came off the bench for his senior debut and promptly looked like he belonged, rating 6.8 in an hour that included one driven run down the left that had the Ipswich full-back reaching for a card he never got shown. Soria was one of two academy graduates promoted to the first-team squad two days earlier, alongside CDM Emiliano Bianchi, who is yet to feature. "We've spent real money on Ngumoha and Sauer this year, and I'll spend more when it's right," Jenkins said. "But days like today are the ones that tell you the academy is actually working, not just producing numbers on a spreadsheet. Marco earned that cap. Nobody gave it to him." Soria himself, still catching his breath pitchside, kept it simpler: "I've been dreaming about that since I was eleven years old, watching my dad's bus go past the training ground. I'm not going to pretend it wasn't emotional."

Days like today are the ones that tell you the academy is actually working, not just producing numbers on a spreadsheet. Marco earned that cap. Nobody gave it to him.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

Wrexham head into the new year two points off top spot with a trip to Brighton to come in the first week of January — and, in Soria, one more name for a first-team squad that keeps finding room for the academy graduates alongside the marquee arrivals.

headline: A Christmas Day Scare, Then Amrizi and Obi Send Wrexham Top of the Premier League
dek: Two days after Oliver Hargreaves compared this campaign to Ipswich '62 and Forest '78, Wrexham went and did something neither of those sides could claim at Christmas — top spot, in their first-ever top-flight season.
body_html:
There is no easing into a Christmas Day fixture, and West Ham made sure Wrexham found that out the hard way. Nine minutes in, Callum Doyle and Rio Ngumoha were both caught square as Castellanos ran off the last defender's shoulder and finished low past Bernt Klaverboer, who was making just his sixth appearance of the season in place of the rested Arthur Okonkwo. For a ground that had spent the morning singing carols outside the turnstiles, the Racecourse went quiet fast. "You could feel the crowd deflate a bit," Owen Meredith wrote from the press box. "Nobody wants to be chasing a game on the 25th of December."

They did not stay behind for long. Yacel Amrizi, whose habit of scoring at exactly the moment Wrexham need him to has become the defining trend of this Premier League campaign, levelled things in the 54th minute with the kind of low, first-time finish that has become his signature. Toni Fruk did the unglamorous work to make it happen, and Andrés Gómez — introduced from the bench in the second half — turned provider again for Chido Obi's 80th-minute winner, the teenager's ninth league goal of the season and another reminder of why Jenkins keeps finding minutes for him even with Fruk and Amrizi both firing. "Chido doesn't care what day it is or who's watching," Jenkins said afterward. "He just wants the ball in the box. That's a gift you can't coach into a player."

The Racecourse, Wrexham · Matchday 18
ResultWrexham 2–1 West Ham
ScorersCastellanos 9' (opp.) · Y. Amrizi 54' · C. Obi 80'
B. GutiérrezMan of the Match · 7.8 rating
Premier League TableP18 W12 D3 L3, 39 pts · 1st

The man-of-the-match award, though, belonged to someone who had not featured at all a fortnight ago. Brian Gutiérrez, sidelined with a shoulder knock picked up in the closing stages at Brentford, was passed fit in time to start and produced arguably his best ninety minutes in a Wrexham shirt — a 7.8 rating built on the kind of composed midfield work that let Mokio and Bobadilla push forward without exposing the back line a second time. "Four days off with a shoulder problem and I come back and play my best game of the season," Gutiérrez said, laughing, after the final whistle. "Football doesn't always make sense." Jenkins was less surprised: "Brian's a player who trusts his prep. He came back into a group that had already shown it could win the ugly ones without him — he just made sure this one wasn't ugly for long."

The bigger story sits above the scoreline. Two days earlier, Sky Sports' Oliver Hargreaves had written that Wrexham's first Premier League campaign was already earning comparisons to Ipswich Town's 1961-62 title win and Brian Clough's Nottingham Forest — while being careful to note that Wrexham, at the time of writing, sat second. That footnote is out of date already. With Arsenal and Manchester City both without midweek fixtures over the Christmas period, three points against West Ham was enough to send Wrexham top of the Premier League table on Christmas Day, in their first season in the competition's history. Meredith, watching from the press box, was careful with his framing even in a moment that invited hyperbole: "Top of the table on the 25th of December means precisely nothing about where this team finishes in May. It means everything about how far this club has already come." A West Ham player, asked in the mixed zone what it was like facing a promoted side sitting top of the league, put it more bluntly: "They don't play like a team that's supposed to be here for the first time. Somebody should tell them that."

Four days off with a shoulder problem and I come back and play my best game of the season. Football doesn't always make sense.

— Brian Gutiérrez, post-match

Wrexham are back in action for the trip to Ipswich Town on Boxing Day week, with the fixture list showing no sign of slowing down before the New Year. For a club that spent last Christmas fighting for automatic promotion out of the Championship, sitting top of the Premier League twelve months later is the kind of contrast nobody at the Racecourse is taking for granted just yet.

headline: Second Place After Seventeen Matches: Why Wrexham's First Premier League Campaign Already Belongs in the History Books
dek: Whatever happens between now and May, what Keeyvon Jenkins has built in barely eighteen months at the Racecourse has already crossed a threshold English football rarely sees from a newly promoted club.
body_html:
There is a version of this column that gets written every few years, usually in spring, usually after the fact: a newly promoted club held the line long enough to make the rest of the division briefly nervous, and by the time the final table was printed, the romance had curdled into relief that normal service had resumed. Seventeen matches into their first season in the Premier League, Wrexham are threatening to make me write a different column entirely — and for once, the case does not need much dressing up.

Second in the table. Thirty-six points from seventeen games. A goal difference of plus-23, the best of any side in the division, built on the best defensive record in the league — ten goals conceded, nobody else within seven of them. A run to the Carabao Cup semi-finals that included, three days after a ninetieth-minute league defeat to the same opponent, taking an academy-heavy XI to the Etihad and beating a Manchester City side fielding real first-team players. And underneath all of it, a Championship title from the season before that nobody outside Wrexham seriously expects to be repeated by most clubs who go up in their place.

By the Numbers, After 17 Premier League Matches
League Position2nd, 36 pts
Goal Difference+23 · best in the division
Goals Conceded10 · best defensive record in the league
Cup ProgressCarabao Cup semi-finalists
Prior SeasonEFL Championship champions, 2025–26

Keeyvon Jenkins did not inherit this. He was appointed in January of last year to a club still finding its feet in the Championship, and what he has built since — a defensive record most established top-flight sides would frame on the wall, an academy pipeline producing first-team minutes rather than loan-list fodder, a squad assembled with the kind of coherence that usually takes seasons to establish — did not happen by accident. It is worth being precise about what that comparison actually requires, because English football has only a handful of promoted-club campaigns that earn the historical company Wrexham's form is now inviting.

Brian Clough's Nottingham Forest is the obvious starting point, and the obvious caveat: Forest were promoted in 1977, finished third in their first season back in the old First Division, then won it outright in their second, and followed that with back-to-back European Cups. Nobody sane is promising Wrexham a Clough trajectory — that run remains one of the genuine impossibilities of the English game, a fluke of timing and managerial genius unlikely to be repeated. But the underlying mechanism is recognisable: an unfashionable club, a manager building a specific identity rather than buying one off the shelf, and results that arrive not despite the modesty of the operation but because of the coherence of it. Alf Ramsey's Ipswich Town offers the tighter parallel — promoted in 1961, and remarkably, champions of the entire top flight the very next season, on a tactical setup so far ahead of what the rest of the division had scouted for that opponents spent half the campaign working out what they were even facing. Wrexham's identity under Jenkins is not a secret in the same way Ramsey's wing-less formation was in 1962. But the underlying story — a provincial club punching miles above its transfer budget through tactical coherence and defensive organisation rather than star power — is the same story, told sixty-four years later.

The comparison every reader will reach for regardless is Leicester City's 2015-16 title, and it is worth saying plainly why that one fits less neatly than the other two: Leicester's miracle arrived in their second full season back in the top flight, not their first, and was built on a run of late-season form as much as a season-long defensive identity. Wrexham, seventeen games in, are further ahead of schedule than Leicester were at the same stage of their own story. That is not a prediction. It is an observation, and the two things are not the same.

Whatever happens between now and May — and second place after seventeen games guarantees nothing, least of all a title race against opposition with City's and Arsenal's resources — Wrexham have already produced one of the outstanding opening Premier League campaigns any promoted club has managed in the competition's history.

— Oliver Hargreaves, Sky Sports

None of this requires Wrexham to actually win the league to matter. English football's history is not short of promoted sides who flattered in August and September before the division's superior resources ground them back down by Easter; it is much shorter on sides still holding the best defensive record in the country after seventeen matches, with a run to a domestic cup semi-final and a title in the division below achieved in the same eighteen-month window under the same manager. If Wrexham finish this season second, or fifth, or somewhere the algorithms would call a regression to the mean, that will not erase what these seventeen matches have already put on the record. Some seasons are judged entirely by where they end. This one has already justified itself by where it started.

headline: Nico Kopp Man of the Match Again as Wrexham's Kids See Off Wolves to Win a Third Straight Youth Rush Title
dek: A tighter final than the last two, but the same result — and, remarkably, the same name topping the ratings sheet at full-time as it had four hours earlier in the semi.
body_html:
If Wrexham's academy has made anything look routine this season, it is the closing weeks of the Youth Rush calendar. A 2–0 win over Wolves in the final was a more modest scoreline than the double-digit routs that closed out the previous campaign, but the outcome was never seriously in question. Martin Leon opened the scoring from a tight angle he has been practising in training for weeks, according to academy staff, and Nathaniel Matthews doubled the lead before the hour — his first involvement of a final that, for long stretches, Wolves' back line spent simply trying to survive.

The story of the day, though, belonged between the posts. Nico Kopp, the German goalkeeper who has quietly become the most talked-about name in the academy's development meetings, followed a man-of-the-match display in the afternoon's semi-final with another one in the final — two commanding performances in the space of a single day that left Owen Meredith's notebook short on comparisons. "You don't usually get a goalkeeper man-of-the-match twice in one afternoon," Meredith wrote pitchside. "Kopp made it look almost unremarkable, which is its own kind of remarkable."

Youth Rush Tournament Final, Neutral Venue
ResultWrexham 2–0 Wolves
ScorersM. Leon · N. Matthews
N. Kopp, 17Man of the Match · 7.8 rating
Trophy CountThree straight Youth Rush titles

Two man-of-the-match performances in one day from a goalkeeper is not something you plan for. It's just something special that's happening with that kid right now.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

Three finals, three trophies — the Rush campaign has stopped being a proving ground for Wrexham's academy and started looking like a formality the group is simply expected to clear on the way to bigger things. Jenkins, asked afterward whether the run was becoming easy to take for granted, was careful not to let it: "It's easy to look at the scorelines and assume it's simple. It isn't. Winning three finals in a row at that age takes real character, and I don't want anyone at this club treating it like it's owed to us."

headline: Valentino Martini's Hat-Trick From Centre-Back Sends Wrexham's Kids Past Brentford and Into the Final
dek: A centre-back doesn't usually headline a semi-final report. Today, nobody in the press box was arguing with the exception.
body_html:
Valentino Martini has spent his time in Wrexham's academy being talked about for his reading of the game, not his finishing — a Ball-Playing Defender by trade, more likely to start a move than end one. That reputation took a battering in the best possible way against Brentford, as the Italian teenager scored three times from sat-piece situations and open play alike in a 4–1 semi-final win that sent Wrexham through to a third straight Youth Rush final. Nathan Salaun added the fourth, a tidy finish that will have done his own case for more minutes no harm at all.

Behind it all, Nico Kopp produced the kind of performance that makes academy staff sit up in meetings: a 9.8 rating and the match ball's worth of big saves that kept Brentford's one moment of real quality from becoming two. "Val's not going to become a striker overnight, and that's fine," Jenkins said afterward, smiling. "But that's the calibre of player we're developing across this whole group now — even the ones we build the team around defensively can produce an afternoon like that." Martini himself, still visibly surprised by his own hat-trick, put it more simply: "I don't really know what happened. The ball kept finding me and I kept putting it in."

— Valentino Martini, post-match

headline: Jules Collin's Brace Opens a New Youth Rush Campaign With a 3–1 Win Over Crystal Palace
dek: A tighter opener than the last one, with Mika Horn called into real action for the first time all campaign — and answering the call.
body_html:
Wrexham's academy opened the newest edition of the Youth Rush Tournament the way it has closed out the last two — with Jules Collin on the scoresheet. The French winger scored twice and set up Stéphane Bertrand's opener in a 3–1 win over Crystal Palace that was, for the first time in a while, a genuine contest rather than a formality; Palace's academy pushed back hard enough in the second half to force a real save or two out of Mika Horn, who repaid the trust with an 8.0-rated afternoon between the posts and the tournament's early man-of-the-match award.

Ben Forster's assist rounded out the scoring involvement, while the rest of the group treated the win as exactly the kind of business-like start Jenkins has come to expect from this group heading into a knockout day. "Palace made us work for it more than we're used to in this competition," Jenkins said afterward. "That's not a bad thing. It's good preparation for two more knockout matches on the same afternoon." Nobody in the camp seemed especially worried about the closer scoreline — not with a semi-final and, potentially, a third straight final still to come before the day was out.
