headline: Three Days After Reijnders Broke Their Hearts, Wrexham's Kids Go to the Etihad and Beat Manchester City's Best
dek: Saturday's ninetieth-minute sucker-punch was still fresh when the teamsheets went up for a Carabao Cup quarter-final nobody outside the building expected Wrexham to take seriously. City took it seriously. Wrexham took the result.
date_line: December 15, 2026 · Etihad Stadium, Manchester
body_html:
Three days is not very long to get over a goal like Tijjani Reijnders'. Owen Meredith was still writing about the Racecourse's stunned final whistle from Saturday's 1–2 when the club bus pulled out for Manchester again, this time for a Carabao Cup quarter-final that plenty of neutrals had already filed under "dead rubber" — the kind of midweek fixture a newly promoted side is expected to use for squad rotation and not much else. Manchester City, notably, did not treat it that way. Pep Guardiola named a team with real senior quality in it, the sort of selection that says a club still wants the trophy rather than one going through the motions. Keeyvon Jenkins, for his part, sent out a Wrexham XI built almost entirely around academy graduates and squad players who rarely feature in the Premier League picture. On paper, four days after a heartbreak against City's actual first team, this looked like the kind of week that could break a promoted club's spirit rather than restore it.

It did the opposite. Juan Cruz Vargas, who has made a habit this season of finding the net from the bench, broke the deadlock in the 40th minute with a finish that owed as much to composure as anything else — the same calm City's more expensive attackers had lacked three days earlier at the other end of the M56. Chido Obi, the teenager who promised in August that Wrexham "wasn't scared of the prestige of this league," made good on the words from the penalty spot in the 66th, sending the away end at the Etihad into a noise usually reserved for occasions considerably bigger than a midweek cup tie. Two goals, a clean sheet, and a Wrexham XI that had barely featured together before kickoff walked off having beaten a City side with real first-team players in it — on the same ground, in the same week, as the club that had just denied them at the death.

Etihad Stadium, Manchester · Carabao Cup Quarter Final
ResultManchester City 0–2 Wrexham
J.C. VargasGoal, 40' · 7.0 rating
C. ObiGoal (pen), 66' · Man of the Match, 7.6 rating
Turnaround3 days after a 1–2 league defeat to the same club

The names on the teamsheet told their own story. Jorthy Mokio and Jamal Belghazi anchored a back line completed by Andrés Cuenca and Elijah Dijkstra, neither a regular in the league side, while Max Cleworth and Mario Barbieri covered positions usually reserved for Wrexham's first-choice full-backs. Bernt Klaverboer kept a clean sheet in goal against a front line that, three days earlier, had needed a ninetieth-minute moment of individual brilliance to get past a very similar defensive shape. Leo Sauer and Vladyslav Veleten ran City's rotated full-backs into the ground on the flanks. It was, by a distance, the least experienced XI Jenkins has fielded against top-flight opposition all season. It played like the opposite.

Saturday hurt. I told this group before kickoff that the only answer to a result like that is another result, and it doesn't matter that it's a different set of players doing the answering — it's still this club, still this badge. They went out and got it done against a team with real players in it. I couldn't be prouder of that dressing room this week.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

"There is a version of this fixture list that would have broken a lesser club's week — the same opponent, the same stadium, six days apart, the first result as cruel as football gets," Meredith wrote afterward. "Wrexham's response to that version was to send out their academy and win anyway." A City player, asked about the result in the mixed zone, was blunter: "We didn't take it lightly and we still lost. Whatever they're building at that club, it's not just the first team." The Racecourse gets its next league fixture at the weekend, still processing a week that delivered its worst ninety minutes of the season and one of its best inside the same seventy-two hours.

headline: Sauer's Stoppage-Time Penalty Seals It as Wrexham Survive a Scare at Brentford to Go Second
dek: A week after the City heartbreak, Wrexham needed a nervy, error-strewn ninety to keep pace at the top — and got the job done in exactly the manner Jenkins didn't want them to.
date_line: December 19, 2026 · Gtech Community Stadium, Brentford
body_html:
If last Saturday's near-miss against Manchester City was Wrexham at their most composed, this was the opposite fixture in almost every respect. Damián Bobadilla put the visitors ahead in the 26th minute with the kind of driven finish from the edge of the box that has become his trademark this season, and for the best part of an hour Wrexham looked in control of a game that, on paper, they were expected to be in control of. Chido Obi doubled the lead not long after, continuing a run of form that has made him close to undroppable off the bench, and the travelling end had settled in for a comfortable afternoon at the Gtech Community Stadium. Then the concentration that has defined so much of this Premier League campaign went missing for twenty minutes, and Brentford made them pay for it.

Fabio Janelt's 63rd-minute strike, from a move Wrexham's back line will want to forget in the video review, turned a laboured stroll into a genuine contest, and Arthur Okonkwo — recalled in goal after Bernt Klaverboer's recent run of cup appearances — endured one of his roughest afternoons of the season, finishing with a 5.4 rating that reflected a defence under far more sustained pressure than the scoreline eventually suggested. "We took our foot off it for twenty minutes and a team like Brentford will make you regret that," Jenkins admitted afterward. "We got away with it today. We won't always." It took until the fourth minute of stoppage time for the visitors to finally settle it, Leo Sauer sending the home goalkeeper the wrong way from the penalty spot after Obi was caught late in the box — a cool finish under real pressure that Sauer himself downplayed in the mixed zone: "I've practised that same run-up a hundred times in training. In that moment, you just trust it."

Gtech Community Stadium, Brentford · Matchday 17
ResultBrentford 1–3 Wrexham
ScorersD. Bobadilla 26' · C. Obi · F. Janelt 63' (opp.) · L. Sauer 90' (pen)
Wrexham's BestL. Cacace, 7.5 rating
Premier League TableP17 W11 D3 L3, 36 pts · 2nd

We took our foot off it for twenty minutes and a team like Brentford will make you regret that. We got away with it today. We won't always.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

There was a sourer note to the afternoon away from the scoreline. Brian Gutiérrez, who had come on and was still finding his rhythm in midfield, went down clutching his shoulder late on and did not finish the match; the club described it afterward as a knock expected to keep him out for roughly four days rather than anything more serious, but it is the kind of fixture-list scare Jenkins can do without with the schedule about to compress around the Christmas period. Elsewhere, Liberato Cacace's 7.5 rating at right-back was the most complete individual performance of the afternoon, a reminder of how thoroughly his conversion from left-back has paid off this season, while Juan Cruz Vargas's introduction from the bench produced little of the late magic he has become known for — a quiet 5.9 on a day when the headline moments belonged to others. Owen Meredith, watching from the press box, put the result in its proper context afterward: "Wrexham didn't play like the second-best team in England today. They played like a good team that got its result anyway. At this point in a first Premier League season, I'm not sure anyone at that club minds which version shows up, as long as the three points do." The win moves Wrexham above Manchester City on goal difference and back into the Champions League places heading into the Christmas fixtures, with West Ham due at the Racecourse next.

headline: Reijnders' 90th-Minute Winner Denies Wrexham a Famous Night as Manchester City Reclaim Top Spot
dek: Six days after Owen Meredith wrote that Manchester City's visit would answer the season's real question, the Racecourse got ninety minutes of an answer it didn't want — settled, cruelly, in the final minute of stoppage time.
body_html:
Erling Haaland needed nineteen minutes to remind the Racecourse exactly why he leads the Premier League's scoring charts, ghosting off Ayden Heaven's shoulder to finish a low cross first time and silence a crowd that had spent the first quarter-hour daring to believe. What followed was the best forty-five minutes of pure defiance this ground has produced all season. Rio Ngumoha, deployed as a floating left-sided threat all afternoon, cut inside two City defenders in the 36th minute and drilled a finish into the far corner that sent the home end into a noise Meredith described in his notes as "somewhere between relief and disbelief." For the rest of the half and the better part of the second, City — top of the table on goal difference alone before kickoff — could not find a second gear against a Wrexham side that defended in numbers and broke with real purpose. "I told the group at half-time that if we could hold that line for another forty-five, we'd have done something nobody expected of us in our first season up here," Jenkins said afterward, his voice still carrying the game's tension well into the press conference. "For eighty-nine minutes, we did."

The ninetieth is where it fell apart. Tijjani Reijnders, introduced only twelve minutes earlier, arrived unmarked at the back post to turn in a cutback that Callum Doyle — rated 7.2 on an afternoon he'd otherwise controlled — will replay more than once this week, and the away end that had gone largely quiet for an hour erupted as Wrexham's players sank to the turf around him. "It's the cruellest way to lose a match like that," Ngumoha said in the mixed zone, still catching his breath. "We matched them. Everybody in that stadium saw we matched them. One mistake in the ninetieth minute and it's gone. That's football, but it doesn't make it hurt less tonight." A City player, magnanimous in victory, offered a version of the same respect from the other dressing room: "That was one of the hardest away days we've had all season. They didn't look like a promoted side out there. Fair play to them."

The Racecourse, Matchday 16
ResultWrexham 1–2 Manchester City
ScorersE. Haaland 19' (opp.) · R. Ngumoha 36' · T. Reijnders 90' (opp.)
Wrexham's BestA. Heaven, 7.4 rating
Premier League TableP16 W10 D3 L3, 33 pts · 3rd

Last-minute goal, that's the story tonight, and it crushed the hopes of what could've been a real Wrexham shocker. But we have to hang our heads high after a game like that. We showed them we're not intimidated by the talent on the other side. We have talent too, and we're here to stay.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

The table now reads Manchester City top on 36, Arsenal second on 35, and Wrexham third on 33 — level on points with the total they carried into kickoff, a reminder that this result, for all its late-drama, cost the club exactly nothing in the standings beyond the psychological weight of a night that had briefly felt within reach. Meredith's column has spent four months circling the same question about whether this squad, built as fast and as young as it was, could live with the division's genuine superpowers over ninety minutes rather than in flashes. Saturday supplied the closest thing to a real answer yet: not a win, but not the gulf-in-class evening some pre-match previews had quietly expected either. Toni Fruk's assist for Ngumoha's goal took his tally to five for the campaign, and Arthur Okonkwo — beaten twice but otherwise repeatedly called upon — will take limited comfort from a night that nonetheless kept the concession count to what it was against a front line this dangerous. Brentford visit the Racecourse in a week, a fixture Jenkins will need his players to treat as routine business rather than a comedown from Saturday's near-miss.

headline: The Ninety Minutes I'll Think About All Week
dek: Four matchdays since the last one of these — three wins and now a loss that stings more than any of the wins felt good.
body_html:
I've written in here before about not letting one result define a stretch, and I still believe that, but I'm not going to pretend tonight doesn't sit differently than the Sunderland or Leeds games did. We led the league table for six days. Six days. Fifteen years outside the Football League and we got six days at the top of the Premier League, and I let myself enjoy about four of them before City reminded us why they're City. Haaland's goal in the nineteenth minute was the kind you can't really coach against — a finish that good is just a finish that good. What we did after that, though, was ours. Forty-five minutes of the best defensive shape this squad has shown all season, and Rio Ngumoha's equalizer was the kind of moment I want this group building its identity around: not intimidated, not happy just to be there.

Then the ninetieth minute happened, and I keep coming back to the same uncomfortable thought — we didn't lose that game to a better team playing better football for ninety minutes. We lost it to one mistake, in one moment, against a squad with the individual quality to make you pay for exactly one mistake. That's the gap between where we are and where they are right now. It isn't the gulf people expected in August. It's smaller than that. But it's still there, and closing the rest of it is going to take more than heart and organization — eventually it takes players who can produce a Reijnders moment of our own, in our favor, in the ninetieth minute of a game like that.

We didn't lose to a better team tonight. We lost to one mistake. That gap is smaller than it used to be, but closing what's left of it is the whole job now.

— KJ

headline: Vargas Strikes Late Again as Wrexham Scrape Past Leeds and Reach the Top of the Table
dek: A near-hour of stalemate, a goal that should have settled it, a sucker-punch equalizer with three minutes left — and then, for the second time in three matches, Juan Cruz Vargas came off the bench to be the last man standing at the final whistle.
date_line: December 6, 2026 · Elland Road, Leeds
body_html:
Yacel Amrizi did what Yacel Amrizi does in the 50th minute, ghosting between two Leeds centre-backs to turn home a low ball from Chido Obi — a rare start up front alongside him — and for the better part of forty minutes afterward it looked like exactly the kind of workmanlike away win Jenkins has been asking his squad to bank against unglamorous mid-table opposition. Then Leeds substitute Joseph rose unmarked at the back post in the 87th minute to level it, and Elland Road, quiet for most of the afternoon, remembered how to make noise. "I thought we'd nicked it and then, typical away day, they find a way back in," Jenkins admitted afterward, the frustration still audible even with the result safely in hand. "That's the Championship in you talking, thinking a one-goal lead at 86 minutes is a job done. It isn't. Not up here."

It took ninety seconds for Wrexham to answer. Vargas, on for his second substitute cameo since breaking into the first team last month, drove into the box and squeezed a finish past the Leeds goalkeeper in the 88th minute — a near-carbon copy of the Nottingham Forest introduction that had already made him a name Jenkins keeps returning to in these post-match rooms. "He's got a knack for finding the moment," Jenkins said, not quite managing to hide how much he was enjoying saying it. "Twice now off the bench, twice in the biggest minute of the game. That's not luck anymore." Vargas himself, still catching his breath in the mixed zone, kept it simple: "I just want minutes. When I get them, I try to make them count." A Leeds player, less pleased with how the afternoon had ended, offered the view from the other technical area: "We were seconds from a point we'd have taken all day. Gutted isn't strong enough."

Elland Road, Matchday 15
ResultLeeds United 1–2 Wrexham
ScorersY. Amrizi 50' · Joseph 87' (Leeds) · J.C. Vargas 88'
Premier LeagueP15 W10 D3 L2, 33 pts · 1st

Twice now off the bench, twice in the biggest minute of the game. That's not luck anymore.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

Buried in the final whistle relief was a number that took a moment to land in the Wrexham away end: three points from Elland Road put the club top of the Premier League table, on goal difference, in the 15th match of a debut top-flight season for a club that spent fifteen years outside the Football League altogether. Owen Meredith, filing from the press box, put it plainly in his notes before the caveats crowded back in: "One hundred and sixty-odd years of history, and this is the first time Wrexham have ever led an English top-flight table — for one week, at least." Manchester City arrive at the Racecourse next, level on points and with a goal difference four shy of Wrexham's own, in a fixture that will do more to answer the season's real question than any result against Sunderland or Leeds ever could. Jenkins, asked directly whether he'd allow himself to enjoy top spot even briefly, gave the answer everyone in the room expected: "Ask me again after City."

headline: Yacel Amrizi's Hat-Trick Buries Sunderland as Wrexham Cruise to a 5–0 Rout
dek: Three days after a workmanlike win at the City Ground, Wrexham needed five minutes at the Racecourse to remind everyone what this squad looks like when Yacel Amrizi decides a game is going to be about him.
body_html:
It took Amrizi five minutes to open the scoring and two more to make it two, and by the time he completed his hat-trick in the 25th minute the afternoon had already curdled for a Sunderland side that looked, by Owen Meredith's count, like a team still adjusting to life back in the Premier League. Damián Bobadilla added a fourth just before the half-hour, and a Trai O'Nien own goal on the hour mark turned a comfortable win into a rout that flattered nobody wearing red and white stripes. "You don't often get a game handed to you in the first five minutes," Jenkins said afterward, trying and mostly failing to keep the satisfaction out of his voice. "Yacel took it and ran. Everything after that was just about not getting sloppy, and to the group's credit, we didn't."

Amrizi's rating of 9.2 was the best of any Wrexham player's season, eclipsing even Bobadilla's hat-trick at St James' Park back in October, and it came with an assist tacked on for good measure — Leo Sauer's second-half tap-in owed almost entirely to a ball Amrizi threaded through a Sunderland back line that had by then stopped closing him down out of what looked like simple exhaustion. "When he gets going like that there's nothing you can do about it as a defender," Sunderland's captain admitted to reporters in the mixed zone, a rare piece of candor from an opposition player after a scoreline this one-sided. "We tried three different markers on him in the first half. Didn't matter which one."

The Racecourse, Matchday 14
ResultWrexham 5–0 Sunderland
ScorersY. Amrizi 5', 7', 25' · D. Bobadilla 38' · T. O'Nien 50' (o.g.)
Man of the MatchY. Amrizi · hat-trick, assist, 9.2 rating
Premier LeagueP14 W9 D3 L2, 30 pts

We tried three different markers on him in the first half. Didn't matter which one.

— Sunderland captain, post-match

Two wins in four days is the kind of stretch that changes how a table looks without anyone needing to say much about it, and Meredith's inbox was already filling with the usual mix of delight and suspicion that follows a Wrexham rout — the sense, familiar by now to anyone who's followed this project since League Two, that supporters still half-expect the good runs to be temporary. Jenkins, for his part, was in no mood to entertain that framing after the final whistle. "Thirty points in December, in our first season up here — I'll let other people worry about whether that's sustainable," he said. "Right now I'm just enjoying watching Yacel play like that." With Bobadilla and Amrizi both firing in the same fortnight, and a fixture list about to turn considerably less forgiving, whether this is the version of Wrexham that shows up in the run to Christmas is the question Meredith intends to keep asking.

headline: A Substitute's First Senior Goal Seals It as Wrexham Ease Past Nottingham Forest
dek: Jenkins warned before kickoff that Forest was "the sort of fixture I've found trickier than the ones against the giants." For an hour, his own words looked prophetic — until a teenager just out of the academy changed the mood entirely.
date_line: November 28, 2026 · City Ground, Nottingham
body_html:
Rio Ngumoha broke the deadlock in the 62nd minute, cutting inside from the left and finding the far corner in a finish that had been coming for most of the second half, and ten minutes later Juan Cruz Vargas — on for his full Premier League debut off the bench, three weeks removed from full-time first-team training — doubled the lead with his first senior goal for the club. Toni Fruk's late assist for Ngumoha's goal earned him the Man of the Match nod, but it was Vargas's name that dominated the post-match mixed zone. "I've been dreaming about that moment since I was a kid watching this club from the stands," Vargas said, still visibly emotional walking off the City Ground pitch. "To score it here, in the Premier League, for Wrexham — I don't have the words yet."

Jenkins, who name-checked Vargas specifically in his own private reflections after the Arsenal draw ten days earlier, was careful afterward not to overstate what one substitute appearance proves. "It's one goal. I know that," he said. "But I also know what it took to get him there — the age-group football, the loan interest we turned down, the patience everyone around this club showed with him. That goal belongs to a lot of people, not just Juan." Owen Meredith, watching from the press box, saw something else in it too: a club whose academy pipeline, so central to the story of its rise from League Two, is still producing first-team contributors even as the marquee Premier League names get most of the headlines. "This is the version of Wrexham the ownership group always said they wanted to build," one match-going supporter told Meredith outside the away end. "Doesn't matter how much money comes in if the kids stop coming through."

City Ground, Matchday 13
ResultNottingham Forest 0–2 Wrexham
ScorersR. Ngumoha 62' · J.C. Vargas 72'
Man of the MatchT. Fruk · assist, 7.8 rating
Premier LeagueP13 W8 D3 L2, 27 pts

I've been dreaming about that moment since I was a kid watching this club from the stands. To score it here, in the Premier League, for Wrexham — I don't have the words yet.

— Juan Cruz Vargas, post-match

It was, by Jenkins's own admission, a comfortable-feeling win rather than a spectacular one — Forest never seriously threatened an equalizer once Ngumoha had broken through, and the away end had time to enjoy Vargas's goal without the usual nerves of a one-goal cushion. But comfortable wins on the road against unpredictable mid-table sides are exactly the kind of results Jenkins has spent the autumn saying this squad needed to start banking, and doing it with a teenage academy graduate's first senior goal attached only sharpens the story Meredith's column keeps circling back to. Sunderland arrive at the Racecourse in three days' time; whether Vargas gets another chance to build on Saturday's cameo, or whether this proves a one-off before he's back in the development squad, is a decision Jenkins will have to make sooner rather than later.

headline: Milán Vitális's Rare Start Delivers a Point as Wrexham and Arsenal Share the Spoils at the Racecourse
dek: The teamsheet went up an hour before kickoff and the loudest reaction in the press box wasn't about Arsenal's front line. It was one name in Wrexham's midfield that hardly anyone had seen there since August.
body_html:
Milán Vitális has made twenty-four appearances for this club since arriving from Slovakia and started, by Owen Meredith's count, fewer than a handful of them in the Premier League. He is the sort of player a squad accumulates rather than builds around — versatile enough to cover two positions, experienced enough not to panic, never quite spectacular enough to force his way past the names Jenkins reaches for first. On Saturday, with Bobadilla managed for fitness and Fruk carrying a knock from training, Vitális got the nod in central midfield against a title-chasing Arsenal side, and turned in the kind of ninety minutes that makes a manager's rotation policy look less like an accident and more like a plan. Man of the Match, by a distance nobody in the press box seriously disputed.

The goal itself belonged to someone with a more familiar name on the scoresheet. Yacel Amrizi rose to head in a Vitális-carried move in the 37th minute, his sixth Premier League goal of the season, and for a half hour either side of half-time the Racecourse allowed itself to believe this could be a statement result against one of the two clubs above them. Arsenal had other ideas. Kepa Barcola equalized four minutes into the second half, ghosting between Doyle and Heaven at the back post from a corner that Wrexham's back line will want back — the one genuine lapse in an otherwise composed defensive performance that saw both centre-backs rated 7.2. "We didn't lose anything today, and there were stretches where we were the better side against genuinely good opposition," Jenkins said afterward, careful with his framing. "But I'd be lying if I said a point at home to Arsenal doesn't sting a little when we had the game in our hands for twenty minutes."

The Racecourse, Matchday 12
ResultWrexham 1–1 Arsenal
ScorersY. Amrizi 37' · K. Barcola 49' (Arsenal)
Man of the MatchM. Vitális · rare Premier League start
Premier League TableP12 W7 D3 L2, 24 pts, 4th

You don't get to twenty-four appearances in a Premier League squad by accident. I've been ready for a chance like this for a while now.

— Milán Vitális, post-match

There is a version of this result that reads as a missed opportunity, and Meredith heard plenty of that version from supporters filing out of the ground — a home game against a side directly above them in the table, a two-goal cushion within touching distance, and a point instead of three. But there is another version that says more about the squad Jenkins has quietly assembled underneath the marquee names: a player who spends most Saturdays on the bench can walk into a match of this magnitude and not look out of place. "Depth is the boring word for it, but that's what won us a promotion and it's what's kept us in this table's top four all autumn," one long-time Racecourse regular told Meredith, unprompted, on the walk back into town. Vitális's afternoon is exactly the kind of evidence that argument needs — and exactly the kind of story the club's academy-first recruitment model, still relatively new to the Premier League stage, will want repeated more than once.

Man City's win elsewhere on Saturday means Wrexham slip from third to fourth, still four points off top spot but now with Arsenal, City and United all sat above them heading into the final third of the calendar year. Next up is a trip to Nottingham Forest on November 28th — a side mid-table and unpredictable, the sort of fixture Jenkins has occasionally found trickier than the ones against the division's giants. Whether Saturday's midfield gamble becomes a one-off or the first sign of a squad Jenkins trusts more broadly than his teamsheet has suggested all season is the question Meredith intends to keep asking.

headline: The Ones Who Don't Start
dek: Five matchdays since the last one of these, and the stretch has been the best five-game run of my time here — with today's team sheet the part I keep coming back to.
body_html:
I wrote last time about a staircase — up, up, up, and then a stumble. Since then it's been almost all staircase. We went to Selhurst Park and put four past Palace. We ground out a one-goal win at home to Villa that wasn't pretty but was exactly the kind of professional performance I've been asking for since preseason. And then Anfield happened, and Leo Sauer decided he was done being a squad player everyone described as "promising." Three wins in a row against a run of fixtures that could easily have gone the other way, and in the middle of it we sold Lewis O'Brien and pushed Juan Cruz Vargas into first-team training the same week — the kind of squad churn that usually costs you a result or two while everyone adjusts. It didn't cost us anything. I'm proud of that more than I've said out loud to the group.

Today was the outlier, and it's the one I want to write about, because a draw at home to Arsenal isn't really the story. Milán Vitális is. I picked him today mostly out of necessity — Bobadilla needed managing, Fruk knocked up in training — and he gave me ninety minutes that made me look twice at how I've been using him. Twenty-four appearances for this club and I could probably count his Premier League starts on one hand before today. That's on me as much as it's a compliment to him. I built a lot of this squad around potential — kids I signed for what they could become rather than what they already were. Vitális is the opposite bet: a finished player, twenty-four years old, who does his job quietly enough that it's easy to forget he's there until you need him and he delivers a Man of the Match performance against a title contender. I don't have a tidy answer yet for how much that should change my selection thinking. But it should change it some.

Depth isn't just insurance against injuries. Today it was the best player on the pitch. I need to stop treating players like Vitális as the ones who don't start and start treating them as the ones I haven't started enough.

— KJ

headline: Leo Sauer's Brace at Anfield Sends Wrexham Third as Liverpool Are Swept Aside 3–0
dek: Twenty minutes before kickoff, the Kop was still doing what the Kop does — scarves up, "You'll Never Walk Alone" rolling down from the stands like weather. By full time it had gone quiet enough to hear the away end sing every one of Leo Sauer's name three times over.
body_html:
It didn't intimidate this one. Wrexham had lost the toss for a slow start at three of their last four away Premier League grounds; here, they simply didn't allow themselves one. Leo Sauer scored twice inside six second-half minutes — the 37th and the 43rd, either side of the half-time whistle in all but the literal sense — and Chido Obi added a stoppage-time third that turned a routine result into an emphatic one. By the time the final whistle went, sections of the Kop had already started filing for the exits, an image Owen Meredith's press-box neighbor from a Merseyside paper called "the loudest silence I've heard at this ground in a decade."

Sauer's performance — two goals, an assist, an 8.3 rating, a Man of the Match award that wasn't seriously contested by anyone else on the pitch — was the kind that changes how a player is talked about inside a building. Twenty years old, Welsh-eligible through a grandparent nobody at the club had bothered to mention publicly until this week, and until Saturday still filed under "promising" more often than "arrived." That filing cabinet needs relabeling now. "I've been telling you for a month that Leo was close to a performance like this," Jenkins said afterward, allowing himself something close to a grin in a press conference he otherwise kept businesslike. "Today he didn't just get close. He got there and then some."

Anfield, Matchday 11
ResultLiverpool 0–3 Wrexham
ScorersL. Sauer 37', 43' · C. Obi 90'
Man of the MatchL. Sauer · 2G 1A, 8.3 rating
Premier League TableP11 W7 D2 L2, 23 pts, 3rd

Today he didn't just get close. He got there and then some.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

There is a version of this club's story that Meredith has been circling in this column since the Hollywood ownership first arrived: the tension between a Wrexham that belongs to a town in north Wales and a Wrexham that now belongs, in some diffuse and slightly uncomfortable sense, to the world. An away win at Anfield, beamed out to whichever country still has FC26 open on a laptop past midnight, is exactly the kind of result that widens that gap further. A woman selling programmes outside the away end put it more plainly than any boardroom strategy document could: "Ten years ago nobody outside this town knew who we were. Now my nephew in Ohio texts me the score before I've even sat down." Inside the away end itself, the noise told its own story — a section that used to be filled almost entirely with red-and-white season-ticket regulars from the Racecourse now carries a visible scattering of American accents and Stateside-bought replica shirts, the strange, slightly surreal residue of a documentary that turned a fifth-tier club into a global object of curiosity. "I flew in from Austin for this one," one supporter, wrapped in a Wrexham scarf bought online rather than at the club shop, told Meredith outside the away end. "Never been to Wales in my life. Feels mad saying that out loud at Anfield."

None of that changes what actually happened on the pitch, and Jenkins was careful in his press conference to keep the two stories separate. But the club's growth off the pitch — the global audience, the reach into the United States, the way a result like this one gets discussed on message boards from Cardiff to California within minutes of the final whistle — is now inseparable from what happens on it, whether anyone at the Racecourse is entirely comfortable with that or not. Whether it stays a source of pride for a proud Welsh institution or eventually curdles into something more complicated is a conversation this column intends to keep having.

The other story from Anfield broke before kickoff rather than during it. Word reached the press box shortly before the teamsheets were confirmed that Wrexham had completed the sale of Lewis O'Brien to Fulham for a reported £5.9m, ending a spell in which the 27-year-old midfielder had drifted from regular starter to squad depth. More striking still was the news that followed it: Juan Cruz Vargas, the 17-year-old Argentine CAM long regarded as the academy's crown jewel, has been promoted to the first team with immediate effect. "This kid has the potential to be special," Jenkins told reporters, asked about the timing of a promotion that lands the same week as an away trip to Anfield. "I want him getting minutes with the first team now, not in six months when it's convenient." Vargas didn't feature at Anfield — a debut this soon would have been a stretch even for a manager as willing to gamble on youth as Jenkins has proven — but the message sent by promoting the club's highest-rated prospect on the same day as a marquee away fixture was not subtle, and it will not be lost on the rest of the academy intake watching from Wrexham.

Three points at Anfield, a Man of the Match performance from a player who spent most of September fighting for a starting shirt, and a teenager with a 90–94 potential ceiling now training with the first team — Meredith's column has had thinner weeks to write about. What comes next, with Arsenal at the Racecourse in a fortnight and a genuinely crowded top four still to be sorted out, is where this stretch of results gets properly tested.

headline: Yacel Amrizi's Second-Half Strike Is Enough as Wrexham Grind Past Aston Villa
dek: For sixty-eight minutes the Racecourse watched a Wrexham side dominate territory, possession and every underlying number that matters without once making a Villa goalkeeper work for a living. Then Yacel Amrizi found the finish the afternoon had been missing, and none of that mattered anymore.
body_html:
"Dominant but no goal" was how the dressing room's own shorthand described the first hour, and it undersold, if anything, quite how one-sided a scoreless Premier League afternoon can be. Wrexham controlled the midfield from the opening whistle, forced Aston Villa into a back-foot afternoon they'll not want to relive on the coach home, and still found themselves level at the break against a Villa side that barely crossed the halfway line with intent. "We had the game, we just didn't have the goal," Jenkins said flatly at half-time — the kind of sentence a manager says a hundred times across a season and hopes never turns into a habit.

It didn't. Amrizi settled it in the 48th minute, ghosting off the last defender's shoulder and finishing with the low, unfussy composure that's become his trademark since the move to Wales — a goal that owed as much to patience as it did to quality, the product of a full hour of Wrexham probing for exactly the gap that finally opened. "We defended really well and controlled the midfield the whole match," Jenkins said afterward, more relaxed once the three points were secured than he'd sounded at the break. "Just took us a while to find the door. Some days you have to keep knocking." Amrizi, typically economical in the mixed zone, put it in fewer words still: "Wasn't pretty. Ball went in. That's the job."

Racecourse Ground, Matchday 10
ResultWrexham 1–0 Aston Villa
ScorerY. Amrizi 48'
Premier League TableP10 W6 D2 L2, 20 pts

We had the game, we just didn't have the goal. Some days you have to keep knocking.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

It's the kind of result that won't feature in any highlight package but that a promoted side needs a handful of across a season regardless — territory dominated, chances created, patience eventually rewarded rather than punished. A supporter queuing at the Kop End turnstiles afterward offered the sort of blunt assessment that tends to travel further than any post-match press conference line: "Watched us miss about eight good chances and thought, here we go again. Then Yacel does that and it's like none of it happened. That's football for you." It's also, increasingly, the kind of grinding, patient, unglamorous three points that separates a Premier League side building toward something durable from one riding a hot run of form — and with Liverpool away next up on the calendar, Jenkins will take a result built on control and stubbornness over one built on fireworks every time.

headline: A Recalled Loanee's Farewell Cameo Helps Wrexham Ease Past Preston North End
dek: Controlled from start to finish, this one was memorable less for the scoreline than for who was standing in goal — a reminder that not every squad decision this window has actually taken effect yet.
date_line: October 28, 2026 · Deepdale
body_html:
There was a small piece of housekeeping buried inside Wrexham's routine 2–0 win at Deepdale that mattered more to the dressing room than the Round of 16 progression itself. Mackenzie Webber, still technically a Wrexham player despite a loan move that has been signed, sealed, and widely assumed complete, started in goal and picked up a 6.3 rating in what could well turn out to be his last appearance in a red shirt before the paperwork finally clears. "He trained like a man who knew this might be it," said one member of the coaching staff afterward, "and then he went and kept a clean sheet anyway."

The football itself was exactly what Keeyvon Jenkins ordered: controlled, unhurried, and largely stress-free. Jorthy Mokio opened the scoring from midfield, Joenathan Amelia doubled it and picked up Man of the Match honours for his trouble, and a front line rotated hard for cup duty — Vladyslav Veleten and Chido Obi both providing assists — did just enough to keep Preston's home crowd quiet without ever needing to find a third. Lewis O'Brien, restored to the middle of the park for a rare start, put in the kind of unfussy 6.8 that doesn't make headlines but keeps a manager's rotation policy looking justified.

Deepdale, Preston · Round of 16
ResultPreston North End 0–2 Wrexham
J. AmeliaMan of the Match · Goal, 7.6 rating
J. MokioGoal, 7.5 rating
M. WebberStarted in goal, contract situation still unresolved

We controlled it from start to finish. Nothing fancy, nothing to worry about — exactly the kind of night the cup is supposed to give you in October.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

Whether Webber's next appearance for the club comes at all is now a question for the club's loan administration rather than its coaching staff. For one Tuesday night in Lancashire, at least, the goalkeeper nobody quite expected to see again put in a shift that Wrexham's progression to the next round didn't strictly need but was glad to have anyway.

headline: Amrizi's Brace Sends Wrexham Fourth as Crystal Palace Are Swept Aside at Selhurst Park
dek: Eight days after a defeat that exposed everything wasteful about this Wrexham side, Selhurst Park got the version that finishes its chances — and picked up an 8.4-rated man of the match in the process.
date_line: October 25, 2026 · Selhurst Park
body_html:
If Owen Meredith's notebook from the Manchester United defeat a week and a half ago was full of "created more, scored less" arithmetic, Selhurst Park offered the opposite lesson entirely. Yacel Amrizi scored twice and finished with an 8.4 rating that made him the easy pick for Man of the Match, Toni Fruk added a goal and an assist of his own, and Andrés Gómez rounded off a 4–0 away win that lifted Wrexham to fourth in the table with matchday nine done.

Damián Bobadilla, so often the headline act in recent weeks, took a supporting role this time — two assists rather than goals of his own — while Jorthy Mokio and Max Cleworth anchored a defence that didn't concede a single meaningful chance all afternoon. "Selhurst Park is never an easy place to play with any swagger," Meredith wrote in his column the next morning, "but for eighty-odd minutes on Sunday, Wrexham made it look like exactly that." Keeyvon Jenkins, typically more measured in public, allowed himself a rare moment of satisfaction afterward.

Last week we created more than we've created all season and had nothing to show for it. Today we didn't need to create as much — we just finished it.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

Fourth place after nine games is exactly the platform this squad's summer spending was supposed to buy, and for one Sunday afternoon in south London, the ledger and the league table finally agreed with each other.

headline: Sandoval's Four Goals Cap a 10–0 Final as Wrexham's Kids Retain the Youth Rush Title
dek: A second straight Rush final ended the same way as the first one did — as a procession — with a new German goalkeeper watching most of it from thirty yards back with nothing to do.
body_html:
There is a rhythm to these finals now. Wrexham's academy walks in as favourites, the opposition's back four spends the first ten minutes finding out why, and by half-time Owen Meredith's notebook has stopped trying to track individual moves and started just counting goals. Arsenal's youth side arrived at the neutral venue on the back of a run that had, by all accounts, impressed people. It did not survive first contact with Fabricio Sandoval, who scored four times inside a game that finished 10–0 and, in doing so, produced the single best individual return of Wrexham's academy season so far.

Sandoval was not alone. Jules Collin added two more to a Rush campaign that has quietly turned him into the pipeline's most reliable finisher, Mathieu Drouet — fifteen years old as of this week and still finding his ceiling — scored once and set up two others, and Marco Soria orchestrated three assists from a wide role that Wrexham's coaching staff have been shaping him toward all year. Emiliano Bianchi, more often a holding presence than a scorer, got his name on the sheet too. In goal, Mika Horn — the German teenager signed into the academy earlier this month — collected a first meaningful appearance behind a defence that barely had to defend, a gentle introduction to life at Wrexham that his development staff will take gladly.

Four goals from Sandoval and I'm still not sure he was our best player today. That's the level this group is at right now.

"You start to run out of ways to say the same thing," Meredith admitted in his own notes after the game — three double-digit-adjacent scorelines in a single day will do that to a press box. But the more interesting story than the scoreline itself might be the goalkeeper standing behind it. Horn cost the club a domestic scouting relationship and very little fuss, and on the evidence of one afternoon with almost nothing to do, Wrexham's academy pipeline at the back is starting to look as deep as the one further up the pitch.

Ben Forster's three assists from midfield did more of the quiet work than the scoreline gives him credit for, and Jules Collin added another to a tally that, across the day's two fixtures, is starting to look genuinely absurd for a sixteen-year-old.

headline: Wasteful Wrexham Made to Pay for Defensive Lapses as Manchester United Leave the Racecourse with All Three Points
dek: Wrexham created more against Manchester United than they had in any match all season and have nothing to show for it beyond a losing scoreline — the kind of afternoon that flatters an opponent's ruthlessness far more than it exposes any real gulf in class.
body_html:
The number that will needle Keeyvon Jenkins longest here isn't the scoreline, it's the expected-goals count: 2.9, by the club analytics staff's own reading, against a Manchester United side that scored twice from considerably less. Yacel Amrizi's 32nd-minute leveler — a low, driven finish that had briefly quieted the away end's early confidence — should have been the platform for a home win against a United team missing some of the swagger that's carried them to the top of the table this season. Instead, two defensive lapses either side of half-time turned a match Wrexham were controlling for long stretches into a first home Premier League defeat since Tottenham back in September. "We had the game," Jenkins said afterward, jaw tight, in a press conference stripped of his usual post-defeat evenness. "We had the ball, we had the moments, and we gave it away twice in ways we don't give it away in training. That's on us, not on how good they are."

United's manager, never one to undersell his own side's ruthlessness, was happy to frame it differently in the tunnel: "Good teams punish mistakes. We've been punishing mistakes all season. Today wasn't complicated." It's the kind of quote Owen Meredith's column has been building toward all autumn — the gap between a Wrexham side that can compete phase-for-phase with the league's best and a Wrexham side that still hasn't learned to close matches out against them. Callum Doyle, exposed for the second of the two United goals, was blunt about it walking off: "We know what happened. We'll watch it back and it won't be complicated to fix, but it needs fixing before it costs us again."

There were individual performances worth salvaging from the wreckage. Liberato Cacace's rating of 7.4 was the best of any Wrexham player on the pitch, a continuation of a autumn that has quietly made the Wide Half-turned-right-back one of the most reliable names in Jenkins's XI regardless of who's missing from midfield. Amrizi's goal was his second of the campaign and came at a moment the side badly needed it, even if it ultimately bought only a few minutes of parity rather than anything more durable. But the story of the day, inescapably, belonged to the two moments Wrexham conceded rather than the many more they created and didn't finish.

We had the game. We had the ball, we had the moments, and we gave it away twice in ways we don't give it away in training. That's on us, not on how good they are.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

Seventh place, fourteen points from eight matches, still comfortably clear of the bottom half of a Premier League table that includes clubs with vastly larger wage bills than Wrexham's — none of that will feel like consolation in the away dressing room's mood tonight, and Jenkins knows it. The town that watched this club climb three divisions in as many years has gotten used to afternoons like the Newcastle rout a fortnight ago; it is less practiced, still, at absorbing afternoons like this one, where the story isn't a lack of quality but a lack of ruthlessness at exactly the moments that separate a genuinely dangerous Premier League side from one still learning how to be one. Whether this becomes a blip or a pattern is the question that will define however many matchdays come next.

headline: One Step Forward, Then Back Again
dek: A month since the last one of these, and the shape of it looks like a staircase — up, up, up, and then a stumble right back to where we started worrying.
body_html:
I wrote in here after Tottenham that the way we responded to that loss would tell me more about this squad than the four wins that came before it. I think I have my answer, and it's a good one, mostly. We went to Stamford Bridge and got a goalkeeper's debut and a clean sheet instead of a second straight defeat. We rotated hard against Bradford in the cup and still put five past them. We scraped a scruffy one at home to Brighton that I'll be honest wasn't our best performance — Bobadilla bailed us out there more than the collective did — and then we went to Newcastle and did something I don't think this club has ever done in a Premier League fixture: we controlled a match against a genuinely good side from the first whistle to the last. Bobadilla's hat-trick will get the headlines and deserves them, but that performance was about more than one player finding form at the right time.

And then Manchester United happened, and the staircase went back down a step. Not in the way Tottenham did — we weren't second-best on the pitch today, not really, and 2.9 expected goals against a top-four side tells me the process is sound even when the result isn't. But it's the second time in eight matchdays we've lost at home after playing well enough not to, and if that becomes a pattern rather than a coincidence, it's the difference between finishing seventh and finishing somewhere that actually worries the board. I told the group in the dressing room after the whistle that we don't fix carelessness by feeling worse about ourselves, we fix it by being more careful, and I believe that. I also know I said something close to that after Tottenham and here we are again.

Bobadilla has turned into the player I didn't know we had six months ago. If I'm honest with myself, I built this squad around kids I signed for potential. He's the one making it work right now.

— KJ

headline: Damián Bobadilla's Hat-Trick Runs Riot as Wrexham Put Four Past Newcastle at St James' Park
dek: This was not a smash-and-grab. From the first whistle to the last, Wrexham controlled a match against a side that finished last season in Europe, and by the time Damián Bobadilla completed his hat-trick the away end had long since stopped believing anyone in black and white was going to spoil it.
date_line: October 4, 2026 · St James' Park, Newcastle
body_html:
Leo Sauer opened the scoring seven minutes into the second half, a composed finish that felt, in the moment, like it might be the story of the day. It wasn't. Damián Bobadilla scored three times in twenty-four second-half minutes — the 58th, the 79th, and the 82nd — to turn a promising away performance into the most complete ninety minutes Wrexham have produced in the Premier League since promotion. "I don't think we've played a match like that away from home at this level," Jenkins said afterward, and for once there was no caveat trailing the sentence. "Controlled the whole thing. Never really in doubt after Leo's goal, and that's not a sentence I expected to say at St James' Park in October."

Bobadilla's rating of 9.1 was the best of any Wrexham player's season to date, and it capped a run of form that's quietly turned a free-agent signing from the summer into arguably the most important attacking outlet in Jenkins's side. "Damián has this way of making the difficult look inevitable," Toni Fruk, who set up the fourth with an assist of his own, said in the mixed zone. "You give him the ball in space and something's going to happen. We just tried to give him the ball in space as much as possible today." A Newcastle source, granted anonymity to speak candidly, put it more bluntly to the local press pack after the final whistle: "We didn't have an answer for him. Nobody in our building expected Wrexham to come here and play like that."

Chido Obi, still rotated carefully through the busiest stretch of the fixture list, added two assists of his own from the bench, while Yacel Amrizi's late strike rounded off a scoreline that undersold, if anything, how comprehensively this game had gone Wrexham's way by the hour mark. It's the kind of result Owen Meredith's column has spent much of this autumn wondering whether this squad was actually capable of producing against a side with genuine European pedigree — not a scrappy win manufactured from limited chances, but a statement built from sustained control. Whether it changes the conversation about what this project can realistically achieve this season is a question for the next few matchdays, not this one.

ResultNewcastle 0–4 Wrexham
ScorersL. Sauer 47' · D. Bobadilla 58', 79', 82'
Man of the MatchD. Bobadilla · hat-trick, 9.1 rating
Premier League TableP7 W4 D2 L1, 14 pts

Damián has this way of making the difficult look inevitable. You give him the ball in space and something's going to happen.

— Toni Fruk, post-match

There will be sterner tests than this one before the season is judged, and Jenkins was careful in his post-match press conference not to let one dominant away performance rewrite the story of a campaign that's still finding its level. But for a club that spent much of September wrestling with the gap between itself and the Premier League's genuine upper class, an afternoon at St James' Park in which that gap simply didn't show up is not a small thing. Bobadilla, walking to the team bus with the match ball tucked under his arm, put the mood as simply as anyone: "Big win. Big performance. Now we do it again."

headline: Bobadilla's Second-Half Strike Edges Wrexham Past Brighton in a Match That Never Found Its Rhythm
dek: Nobody at the Racecourse will remember this one for the football. They'll remember it for the hour Wrexham spent scrapping for a foothold against a well-organized Brighton side, and for the single moment Damián Bobadilla supplied to make sure all that scrapping wasn't for nothing.
body_html:
"We scraped it," Jenkins admitted flatly afterward, in one of the shorter post-match assessments he's given all season, and it was hard to argue with the summary. Brighton came to the Racecourse set up to frustrate, sat compact in midfield, and largely succeeded for the better part of an hour against a Wrexham side that never quite found the rhythm that carried them through September. It took until the 60th minute for the deadlock to break, Damián Bobadilla finding half a yard of space that hadn't been available to anyone else in a red shirt all afternoon and finishing with the composure that's becoming his trademark. "Some days it's not going to be pretty," Bobadilla said afterward, still catching his breath in the tunnel. "You take the three points and you don't apologize for how you got them."

The performance data behind the scenes told its own quieter story — for the first time all season, the club's analysts didn't have full player ratings to work from, a gap in the record that irritated Jenkins more than the performance itself did. "I'd rather know exactly how everyone played today than not know," he said, "but I trust what I saw with my own eyes, and what I saw was a group that ground out a result against a team that didn't make it easy." A Brighton staffer, speaking to the away press pack afterward, was blunter about the balance of the contest: "We came here for a point and we should have got one. Details cost us."

There isn't much more to say about an afternoon this scrappy without overselling it — this was a workmanlike, low-event Premier League win of the kind every promoted side needs a handful of across a season, not the kind anyone puts in a highlight reel. But three points are three points regardless of the manner of their arrival, and Bobadilla's continuing knack for producing exactly the moment his side needs, exactly when they need it, is fast becoming one of the more interesting subplots of Wrexham's autumn — a free transfer quietly turning into indispensable.

Some days it's not going to be pretty. You take the three points and you don't apologize for how you got them.

— Damián Bobadilla, post-match

Owen Meredith's column has spent the last month circling a question about whether this squad's identity is closer to the free-flowing side that beat Wolves in August or the more pragmatic version that shows up when the opposition sits deep and dares Wrexham to break them down. This was Exhibit A for the second version, and not a flattering one — but the ledger only cares about points, and this one goes in the win column same as any other. What it says about the weeks still to come is a question the next fixture will answer better than this one did.

headline: Chido Obi Helps Himself to a Hat-Trick as Wrexham Put Five Past Bradford City
dek: A rotated side away at Bradford barely broke stride, and by the time Joenathan Amelia added a second of his own the only real question left was whether Obi's teenage strike partner would grab a headline of his own before the final whistle.
body_html:
Eleven days after being sold to Barracas Central, the name generating conversation around this Wrexham squad was no longer Mo Faal but the eighteen-year-old who's quietly taken over his old spot in the pecking order. Chido Obi scored three times in a five-goal rout of Bradford City — a 30th-minute opener, a second just after the hour, and a stoppage-time finish that turned a comfortable win into a statement one — and did it against a side that had set up specifically to make his afternoon difficult. It didn't work. "I told him before kickoff that this was his chance to show what he can do against a team that knows exactly what he does," Jenkins said afterward. "He took it about as well as you could ask."

Obi wasn't even the only teenager with two goals to his name by full time. Joenathan Amelia, nominally a right-back for most of this project's life, scored either side of Obi's second to finish with a brace of his own from a more advanced role Jenkins has been experimenting with in cup football — a reminder that the depth chart's neat position labels rarely capture what actually happens once a game kicks off. "I don't think of myself as a striker," Amelia said, smiling, in the tunnel afterward. "But if the gaffer keeps putting me up there and it keeps working, who am I to argue?"

The other story of the afternoon belonged to Andrés Cuenca, handed his first competitive minutes in a Wrexham shirt and repaying the trust with an assist and a 7.7 rating in a display that had the travelling coaching staff nodding along from the touchline. It's the kind of low-stakes cup debut this club has leaned on all year to blood its younger signings without the pressure of a Premier League afternoon attached, and Cuenca looked entirely unbothered by the occasion. Milán Vitális, less happily, picked up a minor elbow knock in the second half that should keep him out for the best part of a week rather than anything longer, according to the club's early assessment.

I don't think of myself as a striker. But if the gaffer keeps putting me up there and it keeps working, who am I to argue?

— Joenathan Amelia, post-match

None of this will make many headlines outside Wales — a heavily rotated League Two trip in the League Cup rarely does — but for a club that has spent this entire calendar year trying to build a squad deep enough to survive the Premier League without leaning on the same eleven names every week, an afternoon like this one is closer to the point than it looks. Faal's sale closed one chapter of that project; Obi's hat-trick, scored by a player who didn't exist on this club's radar twelve months ago, opened another. Jenkins, asked whether he was worried about burying a striker of Obi's age in cup football rather than saving him for the league, wasn't having it: "Good players don't need protecting from games like this. They need games like this."

headline: A New Goalkeeper's Quiet Debut Steadies Wrexham to a Point at Stamford Bridge
dek: A week after the first home league defeat of the Jenkins era, Wrexham didn't need a hero at Stamford Bridge — just a goalkeeper who'd never played a competitive minute for the club making the saves he needed to make.
date_line: September 19, 2026 · Stamford Bridge, London
body_html:
Bernt Klaverboer's Wrexham career began the way most Premier League goalkeeping debuts should and rarely do: without much drama at all. Signed from Burnley on transfer deadline day as senior cover behind Arthur Okonkwo, the German got the nod at Stamford Bridge in what was framed pre-match as a rotation call and turned, by full time, into the story of the afternoon — a calm, largely untroubled 6.9-rated shift that helped Wrexham hold out for a goalless draw against a Chelsea side that had the better of possession for long stretches without ever really threatening to make it count.

"You dream about your first Premier League game being somewhere like this, and you also dream about it being a bit less nervy than it actually is," Klaverboer said afterward, laughing, still in his kit in the away dressing room. "I think I touched the ball four times in the first twenty minutes. That's its own kind of pressure." Jenkins was more direct about what the performance meant for a goalkeeping position that had been a one-man band since the club's promotion: "Arthur's been outstanding for us and nothing changes there, but you can't run a Premier League season on one goalkeeper's fitness holding up forever. Today told me we don't have to."

Chelsea's front line, missing a little of the sharpness that undid Wrexham at home to Tottenham a week earlier, spent large portions of the second half probing without finding the gap that had opened up so easily against Kudus. Toni Fruk and Rio Ngumoha both had half-chances on the counter that a sharper finishing touch might have turned into something more, and Liberato Cacace's continued conversion to right-back produced arguably Wrexham's best individual performance of the afternoon in an unglamorous, low-event sense — the kind of shift that doesn't generate highlights but keeps a back line organized against a side with more raw attacking talent on the pitch.

ResultChelsea 0–0 Wrexham
DebutB. Klaverboer · 6.9 rating, clean sheet
Premier League TableP5 W2 D2 L1, 8 pts

Arthur's been outstanding for us and nothing changes there, but you can't run a Premier League season on one goalkeeper's fitness holding up forever. Today told me we don't have to.

— Keeyvon Jenkins, post-match

It's a quieter kind of story than the ones this column usually gravitates toward — no goals, no controversy, no teenage prodigy stealing the show — but Owen Meredith's running thread about whether this squad has the depth to survive a genuine Premier League campaign got a small, useful data point on a night in West London. A club-record fee brought Klaverboer here to be insurance, not a headline. On this evidence, the insurance is sound. Whether that's enough to satisfy a fanbase that watched their side lose at home just a week earlier is a separate question, and one this point alone won't fully answer.

headline: Kudus Silences the Racecourse Twice as Wrexham Suffer Their First Premier League Defeat
dek: Four matchdays into the top flight, the unbeaten run and the perfect home record both ended on the same Friday night — and one of them had never happened to Keeyvon Jenkins in the league before, home or away.
body_html:
For three matchdays, the Racecourse Ground had been the one constant in a Premier League campaign that everyone connected to Wrexham kept describing, carefully, as "too good to be true." Then Mohammed Kudus arrived and made the case that it was. His first goal, in the 42nd minute, was a finish so unhurried it looked rehearsed — cutting inside Jorthy Mokio, who had otherwise been the best player on the pitch in a rare bright spot for a home side that spent long stretches of the second half chasing shadows, and curling a shot past Arthur Okonkwo that the goalkeeper barely moved for. The second, in the 63rd, was more of the same: patient, inevitable, delivered by a player who looked, for ninety minutes, like he was competing in a different league to everyone else wearing red.

Jenkins didn't reach for excuses afterward, which by now is close to a signature of his post-match routine whether the result is good or bad. "We got beaten by a better team tonight, and a player who's better than anyone we had on the pitch," he said, flatly, in a press room that had grown used to him leaving with a smile. "That's allowed to happen in this league. What isn't allowed is us forgetting how to play the way we've been playing because of one bad night." Andrés Gómez, who had a quieter afternoon than his 6.7 rating even suggests, put it more bluntly in the mixed zone: "He scored twice and we still had chances. We just didn't take them. That's on us, not just him."

The historical footnote will matter more to the people who keep the club's ledgers than it did to anyone in the away end celebrating Tottenham's third-choice striker option finding this kind of form, but it's real: this is the first home defeat of Jenkins's Wrexham tenure in any league competition — the only previous loss at the Racecourse under him came in last August's Carabao Cup exit to Blackburn Rovers, a cup tie the club treated as a squad-rotation exercise at the time. There is no such excuse available tonight. Wrexham fielded close to a full-strength side, and a full-strength side lost.
